Dear Shareholders,
regional markets adapted to new economic realities. Strategic protectionist measures in major economies, including refined tariff structures and environmental trade mechanisms like the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) continued to reshape global trade flows and elevate the importance of low-carbon manufacturing.
I am deeply honoured and privileged to have the opportunity to address you and present the 54th Annual Report of Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL) for the Financial Year 2025– 26. On behalf of the Board of Directors and the entire SAIL family, I extend my warmest greetings to each one of you & sincerely hope that you, your families, and your loved ones are enjoying good health, peace, and high spirits.

Amidst this international backdrop, India maintained its position as a primary engine of global economic growth and one of the world’s fastest-growing steel market. The domestic economic environment remained robust, supported by strong macroeconomic fundamentals, healthy domestic consumption, and prudent policy frameworks. The Government of India’s continued emphasis on nation- building served as a primary demand driver for the steel sector. Public infrastructure investments were further bolstered by the Union Budget’s capital expenditure allocation, which accelerated major national projects across high-speed transport networks, freight corridors, urban transit systems, and maritime infrastructure.

The Financial Year gone by was defined by dynamic geopolitical developments, evolving global trade paradigms, and shifting macroeconomic realities. Across major industrial economies, corporate entities were called upon to demonstrate high levels of resilience, strategic foresight, and operational flexibility. I am proud to share that your Company navigated these complex global conditions with characteristic fortitude, operational agility, and an unwavering dedication to national progress. By maintaining a sharp focus on structural strengths, operational discipline, cost optimization, and forward-looking technological investments, SAIL has fortified its market position and has laid a solid foundation for sustainable, long-term growth.
Furthermore, strong automotive demand, expanding industrial capacity, and vibrant real estate activity contributed to a robust expansion in domestic steel consumption. Under the overarching vision of Viksit Bharat 2047 and the strategic framework of the National Steel Policy, the domestic steel industry continues its steady progress toward long-term growth and decarbonization targets. Your Company remains uniquely positioned at the center of this transformation, providing the essential strength required to build modern India’s infrastructure.

The year highlighted the inherent resilience of both the Indian economy and your Company amidst an increasingly complex global environment. Despite heightened geopolitical tensions, dynamic trade landscapes, and volatility in raw material markets & Forex rates impacting the global steel industry, SAIL was able to draw upon its structural core and strategic direction to lay the groundwork for enduring progress. As we reflect on the accomplishments and challenges of the past year, it is evident that your Company’s commitment to operational excellence and national development continues to guide its forward trajectory.
Navigating this dynamic business environment, SAIL delivered a disciplined and strong performance marked by achieving key operational and financial milestones across all operating units. For another consecutive year, your Company surpassed the ₹1-lakh crore milestone, recording a sales turnover of Rs.1,09,966 crore and revenue from operations of Rs.1,10,810 crore. Driven by operational efficiency, enhanced capacity utilization, and judicious cost management, Profit After Tax (PAT) expanded significantly over the previous fiscal to Rs.3,233 crore (~51% growth Y-o-Y). Geopolitical frictions in key regions generated trade uncertainty, while energy price fluctuations and raw material cost shifts created supply chain volatilities across all industries. During the year, SAIL steel was supplied to landmark projects across the country, including high-speed rail corridors, strategic defense platforms, renewable energy installations, mega power projects, national highway expansions, and complex bridge construction. Your Company takes immense pride in serving as the structural backbone of India’s rapid development.

On the production front, SAIL sustained robust operating rates, recording best-ever Crude Steel production of 19.43 million tonnes and Saleable Steel production of 19.18 million tonnes. These production achievements were backed by another best-ever total steel sales of 19.93 million tonnes, underscoring strong domestic market absorption across primary manufacturing and infrastructure sectors. The Company’s focus on optimizing operating parameters yielded steady improvements across key techno-economic indicators. Blast Furnace productivity reached an impressive 2.09 t/m3/day, while specific energy consumption improved to 6.18 GCal/tcs, and the Coke Rate was lowered to 419 kg/ thm, reflecting enhanced process integration and lower operational costs. These achievements were underpinned by a strong culture of continuous improvement embedded across all facets of the Company’s operations.

A core structural advantage for SAIL remains its self-reliance in primary raw materials, which provides crucial protection against global market fluctuations. Captive iron-ore mines fulfilled 100% of the Company’s iron ore requirements during the year, achieving a total production output exceeding 38 million tonnes. To ensure long-term raw material security for future expansion phases, modernization and capacity augmentation projects across key mining assets progressed steadily. Strategic expansion plans at mines including Taldih, Gua, and Rowghat were actively explored to secure quality raw material supplies for decades to come.
The financial health of your Company was significantly reinforced during the year through active debt reduction and strengthened internal accruals. Strategic capital allocation and improved sales enabled the Company to bring its total borrowings down by Rs.5012 crore to Rs.31,922 crore, raising the Net Worth to Rs.58,195 crore and a reduction of around 4,20,000 T in its inventory levels. This prudent financial management improved the Debt-to-Equity ratio to 0.55:1, further strengthening the balance sheet and providing the necessary leverage headroom to fund future Greenfield and Brownfield expansion programs.

Workplace safety remains the highest operational priority across all manufacturing units, captive mines, and project execution sites. Safety initiatives aimed at achieving “Zero Accidents” were reinforced through rigorous training programs, safety audits, and continuous risk assessment protocols. On the human capital front, driven by a skilled workforce of under 50,000 employees, labor productivity increased to an impressive 630 tcs/man/year, demonstrating the dedication and capability of our personnel.

Your Company remains firmly committed to upholding the highest standards of Corporate Governance, in line with its Vision and Core Values. Guided by this philosophy, the Company strives to foster a culture of transparency, accountability, and integrity through robust disclosures and reporting practices that not only comply with the requirements of the Companies Act, 2013, the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) Guidelines, and other applicable statutory and regulatory provisions, but also endeavour to surpass these standards. SAIL is dedicated to promoting ethical conduct across the Organization, with the overarching objective of creating sustainable value for its shareholders and other stakeholders. This commitment is reflected in the Company’s governance framework and policies, which reinforce the principles of transparency, accountability, responsible disclosures, and sound corporate practices.

To maintain a competitive edge and address evolving industrial requirements, SAIL continued to expand its specialized and value-added product portfolio through the dedicated efforts of its Research and Development Centre for Iron & Steel (RDCIS). During the period under review, 28 new steel product grades were successfully developed and commercialized to cater to high-value applications in defense, automotive, energy, and core infrastructure. Key product innovations included high-strength cold-rolled coils, Extra Deep Drawing (EDD) steel for automotive body panels, specialized electrical steels for power transformers, and high-performance DMR 249A plates designed specifically for defense and naval applications.
Market reception for SAIL’s branded offerings remained remarkably strong, supported by an expanding distribution network across both urban centers and tier-2/tier-3 rural markets. Prominent brands such as SAIL SeQR TMT bars and SAILNEX structural sections sustained their market leadership, becoming preferred choices for structural safety, earthquake resistance, and durability in individual home building and corporate construction. The widening of our channel partner ecosystem ensured deeper penetration into regional markets, aligning with the growing consumption demands of semi-urban and rural India.

Concurrently, infrastructure capital expenditures— encompassing targeted Modernization and Addition, Modification & Replacement (AMR) schemes—were successfully executed across integrated steel plants. Capital investments were directed toward revamping Blast Furnaces, rebuilding Coke Oven Batteries, and upgrading finishing mills. These targeted interventions aim to eliminate operational bottlenecks, lower specific energy consumption,

Looking ahead, SAIL remains focused on executing its strategic growth roadmap to expand crude steel production capacity toward ~35 MTPA by FY 2030–31. This multi-phased expansion strategy will be supported by disciplined capital expenditure plans directed toward green capacity creation, adoption of low-carbon technologies, advanced digital enablement, enhanced customer engagement, and deeper integration with retail and MSME ecosystems. Your Company is well-prepared to capitalize on India’s sustained economic expansion and maintain its leadership position in the steel sector.

Deepening its commitment to sustainability, environmental stewardship, and social responsibility, SAIL advanced several decarbonization initiatives aligned with national ‘Net Zero’ targets. Recognizing the critical imperative of reducing the steel industry’s carbon footprint, your Company initiated strategic pilots focusing on hydrogen injection in operational Blast Furnaces, pilot-scale hydrogen-based Direct Reduced Iron (DRI) production, carbon capture technologies, and expanding renewable power generation across plant/unit locations. These forward-looking green steel initiatives reflect SAIL’s commitment to progressive environmental leadership.
The progress achieved by SAIL during the year is the collective outcome of the trust, commitment, and dedication of all its stakeholders. On behalf of the Board of Directors, I extend my heartfelt gratitude to our Shareholders for their continued trust, confidence, and support. I place on record my sincere appreciation to our Customers, Suppliers, Logistics Partners, Financial Institutions, and Bankers for their steadfast partnership and collaboration.

Beyond core industrial activities, Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) programs continued to positively impact millions of lives in communities surrounding our plants/units. Comprehensive CSR initiatives spanning healthcare services, educational support, clean drinking water access, and rural infrastructure development were executed, reaffirming SAIL’s pledge to foster inclusive growth and community well-being.
I express our gratitude to the Government of India, particularly Ministry of Steel, as well as various State Governments and statutory authorities, for their constant guidance, encouragement, and policy support. Finally, I express my deepest appreciation to our dedicated workforce and contractual employees, whose commitment, resilience, and hard work remain the true driving force behind SAIL’s growth and success.

To ensure long-term market competitiveness and build organizational agility, strategic transformation programs delivered measurable progress throughout the year. The PRAVARTANA initiative harnessed artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced data analytics across integrated steel plants, mining operations, supply chains, and procurement networks. By digitizing core operational workflows, PRAVARTANA enabled real-time process monitoring, predictive maintenance, supply chain visibility, and optimized raw material usage, thereby maximizing operational performance.
I look forward to your continued support as we build a stronger, modern, and future-ready SAIL.
Complementing this technological evolution, the SAIL DARPAN initiative restructured human resource framework across the organization. By modernizing HR systems, skill development frameworks, and organizational processes, SAIL DARPAN aligns employee capabilities directly with evolving strategic business priorities. Project DARPAN

Project DARPAN
Project DARPAN (Driving Advancement by Reimagining Performance Assessment & Nurturing) is a flagship HR Transformation initiative of your Company aimed at Modernizing and Digitizing the performance management ecosystem through a comprehensive Continuous Performance Management System (CPMS). The project encompasses five integrated modules-Role Clarity tool, Target Setting tool, Job Family & Specialization Building (CoE) tool, Continuous Performance Management System (CPMS) tool and Performance Dashboards, supported by advanced digital workflows and analytics. Significant progress has been achieved in finalization of Roles & KPAs across the Organization, development and testing of CPMS tools across the Plants/Units, stakeholder consultations, and extensive capacity-building workshops for HR teams and cross section of executives. More than 8000 Roles and 25000 SMART KPAs have been formulated so far, covering more than 9800 executives. Under the project, PMS & Executive Promotion Policy among others are being amended to ensure seamless implementation across the Company. Upon full rollout, Project DARPAN is expected to strengthen accountability, enhance transparency and objectivity in performance management, align individual goals with organizational priorities, and provide data-driven insights for talent development and workforce productivity across SAIL.

Waste Management
In FY 2025–26, SAIL has made considerable progress in waste management, focusing on reducing generation, maximizing reuse, and promoting sustainable utilization of industrial by-products. While your Company achieved a 27% increase in total solid waste utilization compared to last five years, similarly there was a significant increase of 176% in BOF slag utilization, largely by selling from old stocks, thereby underscoring the commitment to circular economy practices.
A major achievement was the commissioning of a 1500 m³/ hr. Additional facilities included Effluent Treatment Plant of 10 KLD capacity at Kiriburu and Barsua Iron Ore Mines and a 10 KLD Sewage Treatment Plant at Barsua Hospital, which safeguard local water bodies and improve sanitation.

The escalation of military conflict in West Asia during February-March 2026, created new disruptions across the global economy. The temporary closure of the Strait of Hormuz directly threatened global energy shipping, as the corridor handles approximately 20% of global liquefied natural gas (LNG) and crude oil supplies. Asian economies face direct exposure to these energy shocks; historical data from 2024 indicates that 84% of the crude oil and 83% of the LNG moving through the strait was destined for Asian markets.

Conversely, trade relations between the U.S. and China experienced more severe friction. By April, 2025, U.S. tariffs on designated Chinese categories peaked at 74%, which prompted China to implement retaliatory tariffs reaching up to 125%. This impasse was partially resolved in October, 2025 through a bilateral trade agreement that initiated reciprocal tariff reductions.
The resulting rise in global energy prices increased shipping costs and led to sharp corrections across international equity markets. According to the IMF World Economic Outlook Update published in July 2026, global GDP growth for 2026 is projected at 3.0%, down slightly from the previous 3.1% forecast. This moderate slowdown reflects the negative impacts of the West Asia conflict, which are being partially offset by strong, technology-driven momentum from artificial intelligence investments and enterprise adoption.

Despite these widespread trade disruptions, the Global economy demonstrated stronger structural resilience throughout CY2025 than initial risk models predicted. Acknowledging this steady momentum, the IMF revised its CY2025 global economic growth estimate upward to 3.5% in its July, 2026 World Economic Outlook Update. In parallel, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) confirmed CY2025 global growth at 3.4% in its June, 2026 reporting, reflecting robust underlying macroeconomic fundamentals.
Concurrently, global headline inflation is projected to rise from 4.1% in 2025 to 4.7% in 2026, indicating that the steady disinflation trend observed since early 2024 has stalled. However, the global financial system has navigated these shocks more effectively than initially feared. Large spikes in energy prices were mitigated by strategic inventory drawdowns, expanded production from non-Gulf oil- producing nations, and proactive demand-management policies.

D. OUTLOOK
International Monetary Fund (IMF) in its July’ 26 Economic Outlook states that risks to the outlook are more balanced than in April, but still tilted to the downside. The possibility of renewed Middle East conflict looms large and could extend commodity price volatility, further threaten supply chains, raise prices, and weigh on financial conditions. Trade fragmentation could accelerate, possibly hurting output and increasing prices. A possible correction in technology-driven expectations adds to the downside risks, whereas eroded policy buffers can amplify those risks. Upside risks stem from a swifter-than-expected normalization in energy markets, stronger-than-expected technology investment, a revival of durable cooperation that lowers trade barriers and structural reform that raises medium-term growth.

As per Economic Survey of India 2025-26, the Global economic environment remained uncertain, shaped by geopolitical tensions, trade disruptions and divergent growth and inflation outcomes across major economies. Looking ahead, while Global uncertainties remain elevated, domestic growth drivers are expected to continue supporting economic activity. With macroeconomic stability in place and ongoing reform efforts, the economy appears well-positioned to sustain growth in the near term. It concludes that India’s medium-term growth potential has strengthened to 7%, positioning the economy on a path of steady expansion amid global uncertainty.

Global steel prices during FY 2025-26 were characterized by a “V-shaped” recovery in Western markets. Prices peaked in early April, 2025, before entering a downward slide. During October to December, 2025, US maintained 50% tariffs and the EU intensified its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). I. IN-HOUSE DESIGN & ENGINEERING
The Centre for Engineering & Technology (CET), an ISO 9001:2015 certified in-house design, engineering, and consultancy arm of SAIL, plays a pivotal role in driving the Company’s growth and modernization initiatives. CET is entrusted with the preparation of investment proposals and execution support for projects across the steel value chain, from mines to finishing, ensuring both sustainability and regulatory compliance, aligning with evolving environmental norms, particularly in the area of carbon emission reduction. CET’s core competencies encompass a wide spectrum of activities including mine planning, mineral beneficiation, ore handling and transportation systems, pelletisation, and integrated material handling solutions. In addition, it provides design and engineering support for Hot Blast Stoves and Slag Granulation Plants associated with Blast Furnace operations. The domain of CET’s expertise further extends to Coke Oven Batteries, Sinter and Pellet Plants, Blast Furnaces (including CDI systems and top recovery turbines), Steel Melting Shops, Ladle Furnaces, Continuous Casting Units, TSCDR systems, Rolling Mills, and associated utility infrastructure. This includes critical facilities such as Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) systems, Power and Oxygen Plants, Pollution Control Systems, and Plant-wide Automation Solutions.

Emphasizing the critical role of technological advancement and process innovation in achieving sustainable growth, SAIL has established a world-class R&D facility in Ranchi. This Research & Development Centre for Iron and Steel (RDCIS) of SAIL is a premier research institution in India specializing in ferrous metallurgy. With more than 300 advanced diagnostic instruments and extensive pilot-scale facilities spread across 15 major laboratories, RDCIS conducts research spanning the complete Iron and Steel production chain - from Raw Materials to Finished Steel products.
In the FY 2025-26, RDCIS successfully completed 26 R&D projects and more than 110 assignments, delivering substantial technical and financial benefits to your Company. i) Fair values hierarchy
Financial assets and financial liabilities measured at fair value in the statement of financial position are categorized into three levels of a fair value hierarchy. The three levels are defined based on the observability of significant inputs to the measurement, as follows:
Level 1: Quoted prices (unadjusted) in active markets for financial instruments.
Level 2: The fair value of financial instruments that are not traded in an active market is determined using valuation techniques which maximise the use of observable market data rely as little as possible on entity specific estimates.
Level 3: If one or more of the significant inputs is not based on observable market data, the instrument is included in level 3.

ii) Risk Management

ii) Risk Management
The Company is exposed to various risks in relation to financial instruments. The Company’s financial asset and liabilities by category, are summarised in note 43 (i). The main types of risks are market risk, credit risk and liquidity risk. The Company’s risk management is co-ordinated at its headquarters, in close cooperation with the Board of Directors, and focuses on actively securing the Company’s short to medium-term cash flows by minimising the exposure to volatile financial markets. Long-term financial investments are managed to generate lasting returns. The Company does not actively engage in the trading of financial assets for speculative purposes nor does it write options. The most significant financial risks to which the Company is exposed are described below.
A) Credit risk
Credit risk is the risk that a counterparty fails to discharge an obligation to the Comapny. The Company is exposed to this risk for various financial instruments, for example by granting loans and receivables to customers, placing deposits, etc. The Company’s maximum exposure to credit risk is limited to the carrying amount of following types financial assets.
- Cash and cash equivalents
- Derivative financial instruments
- Trade receivables
- Other financial assets measured at amortized cost

- Other financial assets measured at amortized cost
The Company continuously monitors defaults of customers and other counterparties, identified either individually or by the Company, and incorporates this information into its credit risk controls. Where available at reasonable cost, external credit ratings and/or reports on customers and other counterparties are obtained and used. The Company’s policy is to deal only with creditworthy counterparties.

a) Credit risk management
Cash and cash equivalent
Credit risk related to cash and cash equivalents is managed by only accepting highly rated banks and diversifying bank deposits and accounts in different banks across the country.
Derivative financial instruments
Credit risk related to derivative financial instruments is also managed by only entering into such arrangement with highly rated banks or financial institutions as counterparties. The company diversifies its holdings with multiple counterparties.
Trade receivables

Trade receivables
Credit risk related to trade receivables are mitigated by taking bank guarantees from customers where credit risk is high. The Company closely monitors the credit-worthiness of the debtors and only sells goods to credit-worthy parties. The Company’s internal systems are configured to define credit limits of customers, thereby limiting the credit risk to pre-calculated amounts.
Other financial assets measured at amortized cost
Other financial assets measured at amortized cost includes loans and advances to employees and others. Credit risk related to these other financial assets is managed by monitoring the recoverability of such amounts continuously, while at the same time internal control system in place ensure the amounts are within defined limits.
b) Expected credit losses
Company provides expected credit losses based on the following;
Trade receivables
The Company recognizes lifetime expected credit losses on trade receivables using a simplified approach and uses historical information to arrive at loss percentage relevant to each category of trade receivables. For descriptive note on trade receivables ageing, refer note 48.4 (B)
Standalone Financial Statements
Other financial assets measured at amortized cost

Other financial assets measured at amortized cost
Company provides for expected credit losses on “loan advances and other than trade receivables” by assessing individual financial instruments for expectation of any credit losses. Since, this category includes loans and receivables of varied natures and purpose, there is no trend that the Company can draw to apply consistently to entire population. For such financial assets, the Company’s policy is to provide for 12 month expected credit losses upon initial recognition and provide for lifetime expected credit losses upon significant increase in credit risk. The Company does not have any expected loss based impairment recognised on such assets considering their low credit risk nature, though incurred loss allowances are disclosed under each sub-category of such financial assets.
B) Liquidity risk

B) Liquidity risk
Prudent liquidity risk management implies maintaining sufficient cash and marketable securities and the availability of funding through an adequate amount of committed credit facilities to meet obligations when due. Due to the nature of the business, the Company maintains flexibility in funding by maintaining availability under committed facilities. Management monitors rolling forecasts of the Company’s liquidity position and cash and cash equivalents on the basis of expected cash flows. The Company takes into account the liquidity of the market in which the entity operates. In addition, the Company’s liquidity management policy involves projecting cash flows in major currencies and considering the level of liquid assets necessary to meet these, monitoring balance sheet liquidity ratios against internal and external regulatory requirements and maintaining debt financing plans.

C) Market Risk

C) Market Risk
a) Foreign currency risk Most of the Company’s transactions are carried out in INR. Exposures to currency exchange rates arise from the Company’s overseas borrowing arrangements, which are primarily denominated in US dollars (USD). To mitigate the Company’s exposure to foreign currency risk, non-INR cash flows are monitored and forward exchange contracts are entered into in accordance with the Company’s risk management policies. Generally, the Company’s risk management procedures distinguish short-term foreign currency cash flows (due within 6 months) from longer-term cash flows (due after 6 months). Where the amounts to be paid and received in a specific currency are expected to largely offset one another, no further hedging activity is undertaken. Forward exchange contracts are mainly entered into for significant long-term foreign currency exposures that are not expected to be offset by other same-currency transactions. The Company’s capital management objectives are

b) Hon’ble SLP filed by the Company (Pertaining to Bokaro Steel Plant) in Hon’ble Supreme Court in respect of dispute
with Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) related to provisional tariff petition of electricity charges for 2009-2014 was dismissed vide order dated 18th January, 2017, keeping the question of law open. The Order of Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) dt.7/8/2013 related to Tariff of 2009-2014 against Petition No.275/GT/2012 was challenged before Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL) (Appeal No.18 of 2014) in which the Company also intervened and order of APTEL is pending. Further, in respect of the civil appeal filed by Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) pertaining to tariff of Financial Year 2004-05 to 2008-09 against the order of the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL), the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India dismissed the appeal vide its Order dated 3rd December, 2018, which also have an effect on future tariff orders in view of consideration of certain parameters for fixation of tariff. Accordingly, State Electricity Regulatory Commission (SERC) was required to finalise the retail tariff as directed by APTEL, the financial implication of which can only be ascertained after the Tariff fixation by SERC. For the State of Jharkhand where the dispute of ₹587.72 crore arises, DVC has filed its Retail Tariff Application in November, 2020 along with application for Annual Revenue Requirement before the Jharkhand State Electricity Regulatory Commission (JSERC) for the period of 2006-07 to 2011-12 and also seeking adjustment of Revenue Gap/Surplus in the period of 2012- 13 to 2014-15. The Company has also filed their objections on 28th December, 2020 to the aforesaid Application of DVC. 47.5 The Ministry of Environment & Forest and Climate Change (MoEF& CC) vide their letter No.- 11-599/ 2014-FC dated 1st April 2015 issued revised Guidelines for diversion of Forest Land for non-forest purpose under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 (FC Act). These revised Guidelines stipulated that in case of existing mining leases having Forest Land (partially or fully), where approval for only a part of forest land has been obtained under the FC Act, the Central Government accorded general approval under Section-2(iii) of the FC Act for the remaining area also to be Forest Land, subject to certain conditions, which includes realising Net Present Value (NPV) for the entire forest land falling in the mining lease, in case NPV of such forest land has not already been realised.
In this matter, as per legal opinion obtained by the Company, Section 2 (iii) of FC Act, 1980 will not apply to Government Corporation and NPV is required to be paid only for that limited area, which has been approved by MoEF& CC and in which mining activities are proposed to be done and not for the entire forest area. The matter of applicability of NPV for total forest land has been challenged by the Company in Hon’ble High Court of Jharkhand. The Hon’ble Court, in its order, has directed to place the matter before Division Bench of this Court.

49.3 As per the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) guideline, the Company is required to contribute up to 30% of Salary (Basic Pay plus Dearness Allowance) in respect of executive employees as superannuation benefits, which may include Contributory Provident Fund, Gratuity, Pension and Post-Superannuation Benefits. Accordingly the Company has made provision for pension benefit for executive employees @ 9% of Salary w.e.f. 1st January, 2007 and @3% of Salary w.e.f. 1st April, 2015. Further, pension benefit for non-executive employees has been provided @ 6% of Salary w.e.f. 1st January, 2012 and @2% of Salary w.e.f. 1st April, 2015. Subsequent to wage revision, the pension benefit for non-executive employees has been provided @ 9% of Salary w.e.f. 1st November, 2021.

Pension Scheme was approved in the Meeting of the Board of Directors held on 9th February, 2017 with modification that from the Financial Year 2015-16 and onwards, the contribution towards Pension shall be measured, as a percentage of Profit Before Tax (PBT) to average Net-worth. If the percentage of PBT to average Net-worth is 8% or above, amount of Pension contribution shall be limited to 9% of Basic Pay plus DA for Executives and 6% of Basic Pay plus DA for Non-executive (@9% w.e.f. 1st November, 2021), else the amount of contribution towards Pension will be reduced proportionately. However, a minimum Pension contribution shall be kept at the rate of 3% and 2 % (@3% w.e.f. 1st November, 2021) of Basic Pay plus DA for Executive and Non-Executive employees respectively even in case of loss during a Financial Year. During the Year ended 31st March, 2026 provision for pension has been made @ 9% for all employees.

49.5 The Company considers the assets of one entire plant as Cash Generating Unit (CGU). The Company internally reviews whether there are any indicators that the carrying amount of assets of CGUs may be impaired on balance sheet date. If any such indicators exist, the asset recoverable amount is estimated as higher of the net selling price and the value in use. Value in use is based on present value of estimated future cash flows expected to arise from the continuing use of an asset and from its disposal at the end of its useful life. An impairment loss is recognised whenever the carrying amounts

(I) The Company has leases for Land, Office Building, Plant & Equipment, Warehouses & related facilities and vehicles.
With the exception of short-term leases and leases of low-value underlying assets, each lease is reflected on the balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. Variable lease payments which do not depend on an index or a rate are excluded from the initial measurement of the lease liability and right of use assets. The Company classifies its right-of-use assets in a consistent manner to its Property, plant and equipment.
Each lease generally imposes a restriction that, unless there is a contractual right for the Company to sublease the asset to another party, the right-of-use asset can only be used by the Company. Some leases contain an option to extend the lease for a further term. The Company is prohibited from selling or pledging the underlying leased assets as security. For leases over office buildings and other premises, the Company must keep those properties in a good state of repair and return the properties in their original condition at the end of the lease. Further, the Company is required to pay maintenance fees in accordance with the lease contracts.

49.10 The inventory of sub-grade iron ore fines (SGFs) generated at the captive mines of the Company were not assigned any value in the books of accounts of the Company till the financial Year ended 31st March 2019, since, the Government of India Notification dated 19th September 2012 prohibited all captive miners from selling such sub-grade fines.

Following the Government of India Order no.F.No.16/30/2019-M.VI dated 16th September 2019 allowing sale of sub- grade iron ore fines, the inventories of sub-grade fines held by the Company gained economic value. In this regard, the Company also obtained opinions from the Additional Solicitor General of India as well as the Expert Advisory Committee (EAC) of Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI). Based on the aforesaid opinions, the Company recognized these inventories as by-product inventory as at 31st March 2020. Since, these inventories were generated over many year, making it impracticable to ascertain the actual valuation, the Company assigned a valuation to such inventories basis average selling price of similar sub-grade fines over the last 36 months as declared by Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM), a Government of India organisation and as adjusted for royalty and other selling costs.

The Company has obtained all clearances including environmental clearance and clearance from Director General of Mines Safety, Government of India. Further, procedural clearances have been obtained from the State Government of Odisha. In the State of Jharkhand, the Company is carrying Subgrade Iron ore Fines inventory of 32.13 Million Tons (as on 31st March 2025: 32.63 Million Tons) valuing ₹3112.01 crore (as on 31st March 2025 valuing ₹ 3161.07 crore) up to 31st March, 2026 at GUA Mines. The evacuation of dumped fines from Duarguiburu lease of Gua Mine has started in FY 2023-24 for captive use, and for Topilore lease, the necessary permissions for dispatch is awaited. Further, during FY 2025-26, a quantity of 506493T (288556T in previous year) has been dispatched from Gua for captive consumption. With respect to sale, the delay is procedural and the management expects to receive the clearances in due course.

The management has been able to sell off such inventories in the state of Odisha. While, on an overall basis during the current and the previous years, there has been movement of 4.26 million tonnes in the volume of such inventories, there is significant market demand for sub-grade fines and the recent sales price trends are indicative of considerable margins over and above the carrying value of such inventories. The management also has plans to set up beneficiation plant in future that will consume significant volume of sub-grade fines annually. Accordingly, in view of the management, there is no adjustment required in the carrying value of these inventories at this stage. The management has also taken an opinion from Additional Solicitor General of India on 06.01.2026.

49.11 The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) had approved the in-principle strategic disinvestment of three SAIL units—Alloy Steels Plant (ASP), Durgapur; Visvesvaraya Iron & Steel Plant (VISP), Bhadravati; and Salem Steel Plant (SSP), Salem—on 27th October 2016. Following this, the SAIL Board endorsed the decision in its 9th

February 2017 meeting and initiated the disinvestment process. Subsequently, the final approval from SAIL Board was obtained on 11th August, 2017. The entire process of Strategic Disinvestment is being overseen by an Inter- Ministerial Group (IMG). The IMG is chaired by Secretary, Department of Public Assets Management (DIPAM) and co-chaired by Secretary (Steel). The Group appointed various Advisors to carry out the process. Despite two attempts for ASP, the process could not progress further due to either non-eligible or no bidders. SAIL is exploring options for performance improvement of ASP.
For VISP, the EOI issued on 4th July 2019 was annulled by IMG due to lack of bidder interest. The Alternative Mechanism (AM), based on recommendations from the Core Group of Secretaries on Disinvestment (CGD), has approved the annulment of EOI, initiation of process for closure of VISP, monetisation of its land preferably through the National Land Management Agency (National Land Monetization Corporation). SAIL Board in its 496th meeting held on 16th January 2023, has in-principle approved the proposal for the same.

In the case of SSP, the EOI issued on 4th July 2019 was similarly annulled as per DIPAM’s letter dated 5th January 2025 due to lack of interest from shortlisted bidders. The SAIL Board approved this annulment in its 509th meeting held on 12th February 2025.
SAIL Board in its meeting dated 30.01.2026, has approved the proposal for withdrawal of VISP and ASP from the strategic disinvestment to DIPAM through Ministry of Steel.
In view of the current status and the various other processes which are underway, no adjustment in these financial statements is considered necessary at this stage.

51.9 The tax on house accommodation perquisite implemented by the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) effective from 1 October 2001.
The Workers Union filed a writ petition bearing no. 2115(w) of 2002 in Hon’ble Kolkata High Court challenged the tax on House accommodation perquisite levied by Income Tax Department. Hon’ble Kolkata High Court has directed vide Interim Order dated 28/01/2002 that the company not to deposit the amount of TDS on house accommodation perquisite with Income Tax department but to keep it separately.
Accordingly, the company has made Fixed Deposit of `45.95 Crore with Scheduled Bank for TDS on House Accomodation perks under section 192 of Income Tax Act,1961. In 2015, Hon’ble Kolkata High Court vacated the writ petition. In absence of any demand after vacation from IT Deptt, Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) on house accommodation perquisites related to non-executive employees has been accounted as liability including interest thereon even though the demand is time barred and the amount is non-recoverable by the tax authorities as on the reporting date.

Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with Reference to Financial Statements

Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with Reference to Financial Statements
6. (i) Terms of Reference:
The terms of reference of Audit Committee of SAIL Board in line with the Regulation 18(3) read with Part C of Schedule-II of SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, include: the primary function to assist the Board of Directors in fulfilling its oversight responsibilities by reviewing the Financial Reports; the Company’s systems of internal financial controls and Risk management systems, Accounting and Legal compliance that Management and the Board have established; review Related Party Transactions in accordance with the Related Party Transaction Policy of the Company; and the Company’s Auditing, Accounting and Financial Reporting process generally.

The information, as required under Regulation 17(7) read with Part-A of Schedule-II of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Obligations, 2015 is placed before the Board. The Agenda, including compliance reports of all the laws applicable to the Company, along with Explanatory Notes is provided to the Board Members in advance. The Board Members take active part in the deliberations in the Board and Board Sub-committee meetings by providing valuable suggestions, advice and guidance on various areas of the Company’s Business, thus adding value to the decision making process. Additional information as sought is provided to the members. The recommendations of the Board Sub-committee meetings are placed before the Board for necessary approval. As an effective post meeting follow-up system, action taken on its decisions is apprised to the Board.

As per Section 178(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC) shall specify the manner for effective evaluation of performance of the Board, its committees and individual directors. The evaluation is to be carried out either by the Board, NRC or by an independent external agency and NRC shall review the implementation and compliance of the evaluation system. Further, Regulation 17(10) & 25(4) of SEBI (LODR) 2015 and the Code for Independent Directors pursuant to Section 149(8) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires the performance evaluation of Independent Directors to decide their continuance or otherwise. The Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) has vide its Notification dated 5th June, 2015 notified exemptions to Government Companies from certain provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 which, inter-alia, provides that Sub Sections (2), (3) & (4) of Section 178 regarding appointment, performance evaluation and remuneration shall not apply to Directors of Government Companies. The appointment of Functional Directors as well as Part Time Non-Official Directors (Independent Directors) on the Board of SAIL is made based on nomination/appointment by Government of India (GOI). (xxxii) Foreign Exchange Risk and Hedging Activities: SAIL adopts a cautious and proactive approach for monitoring

(xxxii) Foreign Exchange Risk and Hedging Activities: SAIL adopts a cautious and proactive approach for monitoring
currency fluctuations and employing hedging strategies to safeguard itself from any adverse impact and to ensure stable, prudent treasury operations aligned with evolving global conditions. SAIL has a well-defined, Foreign Exchange Risk Management (FERM) Policy duly approved by the Board of Directors to address risks mainly from significant USD-denominated financial transactions, most of which relate to import of coking coal. As per the said Policy, coal exposures generally remain un-hedged, though hedging up to 25% may be undertaken based on recommendations of the Forex Risk Management Committee (FRMC), considering market conditions and expert inputs from banks. While short-term Buyer’s Credit Usage is currently ‘Nil’, foreign currency loans for future CAPEX/ MODEX activities may be fully hedged for their entire tenure to mitigate risks and lock in interest arbitrage, as per FERM Policy.

2. Waste Management (Slag, Dust, Plastics, etc)
SAIL has implemented systems to segregate, reuse, and monetize waste. BF Slag is used in cement manufacturing, dust is recycled in sinter plants, and plastics are handled through authorized recyclers. 3 Greenhouse Gas Emissions & Carbon Footprint
Opportunity Reducing emissions aligns with global climate goals and enhances SAIL’s competitiveness in green steel markets. It also opens doors to carbon credits, green bonds, and sustainability-linked incentives.
SAIL is actively advancing its decarbonization agenda across integrated steel plants through key technological interventions such as CDQ, TRT, CDI, and Waste Heat Recovery systems to enhance energy efficiency and reduce fossil fuel dependence. The deployment of walking beam reheating furnaces is optimizing rolling mill operations. On the renewable energy front, SAIL aims to scale its capacity to 384 MW by FY 2028–29, transition to LED lighting, and pilot green hydrogen in steelmaking. R&D efforts are focused on CCUS, low-carbon technologies in collaboration with IITs, and slag utilization to curb indirect emissions. These initiatives are guided by a phased decarbonization roadmap, participation in the PAT scheme, and alignment with the National Green Hydrogen Mission—underscoring SAIL’s commitment to sustainable steel production and national climate objectives.

Across all plants, Continuous Emission Monitoring Systems (CEMS) provided real-time

Across all plants, Continuous Emission Monitoring Systems (CEMS) provided real-time
emission data directly to CPCB and SPCB servers, ensuring transparency, accountability, and strict compliance with environmental norms. These measures reinforced SAIL’s leadership in sustainable industrial practices, setting a benchmark for how steelmaking can harmonize growth with ecological stewardship.
Other initiatives include upgrading pollution control systems by installing advanced
electrostatic precipitators (ESPs), bag filters, wet scrubbers, and dry fog systems. Process optimization measures such as Top Pressure Recovery Turbines (TRT), Coal Dust Injection (CDI), and Coke Dry Quenching (CDQ) are being adopted to minimize emissions. Infrastructure modernization involves commissioning taller coke oven batteries with CDQ and waste heat recovery, along with cleaner reheating furnaces. Material handling is being improved by enclosing conveyors and automating operations to reduce dust. Real- time monitoring is ensured through Continuous Emission Monitoring Systems (CEMS) integrated with a centralized MIS for compliance and audits. SAIL is also focusing on 100% utilization of blast furnace and BOF slag in construction applications to reduce dust from stockpiles. Green belt development is being expanded with native species to enhance dust capture and biodiversity.

Additionally, SAIL has partnered with BHP to explore innovative, low-emission steelmaking
technologies using hydrogen and biochar, supporting long-term decarbonization and PM reduction goals.
The Particulate Matter (PM) emissions from its Integrated Steel Plants for the FY 2025-26
was 0.57 kg/tcs.
Reduction in Specific Water Consumption: SAIL is advancing a robust water conservation
strategy to reduce specific water consumption in its integrated steel plants. The approach centers on maximizing water recycling through closed-loop systems, reverse osmosis, and membrane bioreactors, along with cascading water use across processes. Traditional cooling systems are being replaced with evaporative towers and air-cooled exchangers, while dry quenching and high-efficiency descaling are cutting water use at the source. Smart sensors, flow meters, and regular audits ensure real-time monitoring and rapid leak detection. Rainwater harvesting and groundwater recharge structures are being scaled across facilities.
BRSR
During FY 2025-26, significant initiatives were undertaken to strengthen water conservation

During FY 2025-26, significant initiatives were undertaken to strengthen water conservation
and wastewater management infrastructure. At Bokaro Steel Plant, a new Effluent Treatment and Recirculation System with a capacity of 1,500 m³/hr was commissioned. The facility has been specifically designed on the Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) principle, ensuring that treated wastewater is completely recycled and no processed effluent is discharged into the environment. In mining operations, additional treatment infrastructure was commissioned, including a 10 KLD Sewage Treatment Plant at Barsua Hospital, further strengthening wastewater treatment and reuse capabilities.
These initiatives have delivered measurable and long-term outcomes, with specific
water consumption reducing from 3.83 m³/tcs in FY 2015-16 to 2.85 m³/tcs in FY 2025- 26, demonstrating SAIL’s sustained focus on resource efficiency and responsible water stewardship. Going forward, all upcoming units and expansion projects across SAIL plants are being designed based on the Zero Liquid Discharge concept. SAIL is also pursuing advanced water treatment technologies, maximizing reuse of treated effluents, and undertaking third-party assessments to identify additional opportunities for water conservation and process optimization.
Reduction in CO2 emissions: SAIL is pursuing an aggressive decarbonization strategy

Reduction in CO2 emissions: SAIL is pursuing an aggressive decarbonization strategy
to reduce CO2 emissions in its integrated steel plants. Key technological upgrades include CDQ, TRT, CDI, WHR systems, all aimed at improving energy efficiency and cutting fossil fuel use. Walking beam reheating furnaces are being deployed to optimize rolling mill operations. On the renewable front, SAIL is expanding RE to 384 MW by 2028–29, transitioning to LED lighting, and piloting green hydrogen for steelmaking. R&D efforts focus on Carbon Capture, Utilization & Storage (CCUS), low-carbon technologies in collaboration with IITs, and slag utilization to reduce indirect emissions. These initiatives are backed by a phased decarbonization roadmap, active participation in the PAT scheme, and alignment with the National Green Hydrogen Mission—reinforcing SAIL’s commitment to sustainable steel production and India’s climate goals. The specific CO2 emissions from its ISPs were 2.53 T/tcs against the interim target of 2.41 T/tcs for 2025–26.

b. If yes, what percentage of inputs were sourced sustainably?
Yes, SAIL has well-defined procedures for sustainable sourcing.
SAIL sourced all its inputs sustainably during 2025-26. The sourcing is primarily from its captive mining network for iron ore, limestone, dolomite and coal, and these mines are operated under strict environmental clearance compliance. These measures encompass land restoration, water management, biodiversity safeguards, and afforestation programs, ensuring that raw material extraction remains aligned with sustainability principles.

In addition to its captive resources, SAIL also procures some inputs such as thermal grade coal and coking coal from domestic sources. To complement the domestic inputs, SAIL imports coking coal and limestone from countries that enforce strong environmental regulations. Moreover, SAIL utilizes ferro alloys produced at its own manufacturing unit, further strengthening self-reliance and reducing dependence on external suppliers.
By combining captive resources, domestic sourcing, in-house ferro alloy production, and responsible imports, SAIL is able to align the production chains with sustainable practices.

Under India’s Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016, Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) requires producers, importers, and brand owners to manage the full lifecycle of their plastic packaging, including recycling, reuse, or safe disposal.
As an importer of plastic-packaged goods, SAIL has fully complied with these regulations in 2025–26 by registering all its plants on the Central Pollution Control Board’s (CPCB) centralized EPR portal and securing the necessary certifications. 3. Provide details of instances of engagement with, and actions taken to, address the concerns of vulnerable/ marginalized stakeholder groups.
SAIL’s plants have consistently undertaken initiatives to support the development of Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs) through the organization of Vendor Development Programs (VDPs). In addition, Special Vendor Development Programs
ANNUAL REPORT
2025-26
(SVDPs) have been conducted with a focused objective of fostering an enabling ecosystem for SC/ST entrepreneurs. These programs were organized in collaboration with the National SC-ST Hub Office (NSSHO), with active participation from the Dalit Indian Chamber of Commerce & Industry (DICCI) and the Tribal Indian Chamber of Commerce & Industry (TICCI). During these sessions, participants were briefed on SAIL’s procurement processes, vendor registration procedures, and the specific provisions available for SC/ST and women-owned enterprises.
These engagements also serve to inform vendors about SAIL’s procurement requirements, items earmarked for SC/ST and women vendors, and the benefits extended to MSEs from these communities. SAIL has also actively participated in various conclaves organized by National SC ST Hub Office (NSSHO) to further promote entrepreneurship among SC/ST groups.

To enhance financial awareness, representatives from Invoice Mart are invited to select SVDPs to educate participants on the advantages of bill discounting through the Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS). In FY 2025-26, SAIL successfully conducted 52 VDPs and 29 SVDPs across its plants.
Furthermore, SAIL plants provide ongoing support to local MSEs through mentoring, training, technical assistance, and capacity-building initiatives. To stimulate regional industrial development, SAIL also offers locally based MSMEs— particularly those situated in the same districts as its five Integrated Steel Plants (ISPs)—access to steel at competitive and affordable rates, supported by favorable commercial terms.

10. Briefly describe the waste management practices adopted in your establishments. Describe the strategy adopted by your company to reduce usage of hazardous and toxic chemicals in your products and processes and the practices adopted to manage such wastes.

10. Briefly describe the waste management practices adopted in your establishments. Describe the strategy adopted by your company to reduce usage of hazardous and toxic chemicals in your products and processes and the practices adopted to manage such wastes.
SAIL’s integrated waste management strategy is anchored in its Corporate Environment Policy, which commits to minimising solid waste generation and achieving 100% waste utilisation, guided by the 4Rs principle — Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, and Recover.
Industrial By-Product Utilisation
In FY 2025–26, SAIL achieved a 27% increase in total solid waste utilisation compared to the previous five-year. BOF slag utilisation increased by 176%, driven significantly by the liquidation of old stocks — a major circular economy milestone.
Key highlights include:
• All BFs are equipped with Cast House Slag Granulation Plants (CHSGPs), enabling complete granulation of BF slag for use in cement manufacturing.
• BOF slag is processed for metallic content recovery, which is recycled back into steelmaking; the non-metallic fraction is used as a fluxing agent in BF and sinter making.
• Other wastes — BF flue dust, mill scale, lime/dolo fines, and refractory waste — are either recycled within plants or supplied to external agencies.
Waste-to-Value Innovations
BRSR
• BOF slag for roads: Used extensively for internal roads and rural road construction

• BOF slag for roads: Used extensively for internal roads and rural road construction
• SAIL Refractory Unit, Bhilai: Developed a dry-leaf composting system, converting biodegradable waste into organic manure, reducing dependence on chemical fertilizers.
• Low-carbon cement collaboration: Under LeadIT ITP, SAIL-RDCIS and Cemvision (Sweden) signed an NDA to explore BOF slag beneficiation for low-carbon cement production.
Agricultural Application of Slag
In partnership with ICAR–IARI under the Ministry of Steel, SAIL has developed Steel Slag–Based Value-Added Products (SSBVAPs) for use as soil conditioners. Patent applications have been filed to protect the technology — opening new pathways for slag utilisation in sustainable agriculture.
Hazardous Waste Management
SAIL adheres to the Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016. All hazardous waste is carefully inventoried, quantified, and either disposed of in captive secured landfills or handled through authorised agencies. Wherever feasible, hazardous materials are reused or co-processed to promote circularity.
E-waste and battery waste are disposed of through authorised recyclers. All SAIL plants are registered with CPCB under the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016, and comply with Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) obligations.

E-waste and battery waste are disposed of through authorised recyclers. All SAIL plants are registered with CPCB under the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016, and comply with Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) obligations.
Construction and demolition waste is internally utilised wherever feasible, with residual quantities disposed of through external agencies.
Through technological innovation, process integration, and inter-industry collaboration, SAIL continues to progress toward its objective of zero solid waste to landfill.

1. Corporate Information
They are deconsolidated from the date when control ceases. Profit/(loss) and Other Comprehensive Income (‘OCI’) of subsidiaries acquired or disposed of during the period are recognised from the effective date of acquisition, or up to the effective date of disposal, as applicable. All the consolidated subsidiaries have a consistent reporting date of 31st March, 2026.
Nature of Operation
Steel Authority of India Limited (‘SAIL’ or the ‘Parent Company’), a public sector undertaking conferred with Maharatna status by Government of India and it’s subsidiaries (the Parent Company and its subsidiaries together referred to as the ‘Group’), it’s joint ventures and it’s associate is engaged primarily in steel manufacturing business in the country.

The Group consolidate the financial statements of the parent and its subsidiaries on line by line basis adding together the items of assets, liabilities, equity, income and expenses. Intercompany transactions, balances and unrealised gains on transactions between group companies are eliminated. Unrealised losses are also eliminated unless the transaction provides evidence of an impairment of the transferred asset. Accounting policies of subsidiaries have been changed where necessary to ensure consistency with the policies adopted by the Group.
General information and statement of compliance with Ind AS
The consolidated financial statements of the Group and joint ventures & associate have been prepared in accordance with the Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) prescribed under Section 133 of the Companies Act, 2013, read with Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015 (as amended) and other accounting principles generally accepted in India. The Group has uniformly applied the accounting policies during the periods presented.

Non-controlling interests, presented as part of equity, represent the portion of a subsidiary’s statement of profit and loss and net assets that is not held by the Group. Profit/(loss) and each component of OCI are attributed to the equity holders of the Parent Company and to the non-controlling interests, even if this results in the non-controlling interests having a deficit balance. The Group attributes total comprehensive income or loss of the subsidiaries between the owners of the parent and the non- controlling interests based on their respective ownership interests.
These consolidated financial statements (the ‘financial statements’) for the year ended 31st March, 2026 were approved by the Board of Directors and authorised for issue in their meeting held on 15th May, 2026.

The Group treats transactions with non-controlling interests that do not result in a loss of control, as transactions with equity owners of the group. Such a change in ownership interest results in an adjustment between the carrying amounts of the controlling and non-controlling interests to reflect their relative interests in the subsidiary. Any difference between the amount of the adjustment to non-controlling interests and any consideration paid or received is recognised within equity.

2.1 Functional and Presentation Currency
Spares having useful life of more than one year and having value of Rs. 10 lakh or more in each case, are capitalised under the respective heads as and when available for use. Where an item of property, plant and equipment comprises major components having different useful lives, these components are accounted for as separate items.

2.2 Use of estimates, assumptions and management judgements
Capital work-in-progress comprises of assets in the course of construction for production and/ or supply of goods or services or administrative purposes are carried at cost less any recognised impairment loss. segment as well as those that can be allocated on a reasonable basis. Segment capital expenditure is the total cost incurred during the period to acquire property and equipment and intangible assets.
The extent to which deferred tax assets can be recognized is based on an assessment of the probability of the Company’s future taxable income against which the deferred tax assets can be utilized. In addition, significant judgement is required in assessing the impact of any legal or economic limits.
The Company has eight operating segments: five integrated steel plants and three alloy steel plants, being separate manufacturing units, have been considered reportable operating segments. In identifying these operating segments, management generally considers the Company’s separately identifiable manufacturing operations representing its main operations.
3.21.4 Inventories

3.21.4 Inventories
The Company estimates the cost of inventories taking into account the most reliable evidence, such as cost of materials and overheads considered attributable to the production of such inventories including actual cost of production, etc. Management also estimates the net realisable values of inventories, taking into account the most reliable evidence available at each reporting date. Significant technical and commercial judgements are required to determine the Company’s quality and quantity of inventories. The future realisation of these inventories may be affected by future technology or other market-driven changes that may reduce future selling prices.
Each of these operating segments is managed separately as each has different requirements in terms of technology, raw material and other resources. All inter-segment transfers are carried out at arm’s length prices based on prices charged to unrelated customers in standalone sales of identical goods or services.
In addition, corporate assets which are not directly attributable to the business activities of any operating segment are not allocated to a segment. This primarily applies to the Company’s administrative head office and mining operations.
3.21.5 Defined Benefit Obligation (DBO)
Consolidated Financial Statements

Consolidated Financial Statements
Employee benefit obligations are measured on the basis of actuarial assumptions which include mortality and withdrawal rates as well as assumptions concerning future developments in discount rates, medical cost trends, anticipation of future salary increases and the inflation rate. The Company considers that the assumptions used to measure its obligations are appropriate. However, any changes in these assumptions may have a material impact on the resulting calculations.
There have been no changes from prior periods in the measurement methods used to determine reported segment profit or loss.
3.20 Earnings per share
Basic earnings per share is computed by dividing profit or loss for the year attributable to equity holders by the weighted average number of shares outstanding during the year. Partly paid-up shares are included as fully paid equivalents according to the fraction paid-up.
3.21.6 Fair Value Measurements

3.21.6 Fair Value Measurements
The Company applies valuation techniques to determine the fair value of financial instruments (where active market quotes are not available) and non-financial assets. This involves developing estimates and assumptions consistent with the market participants to price the instrument. The Company’s assumptions are based on observable data as far as possible, otherwise on the best information available. Estimated fair values may vary from the actual prices that would be achieved in an arm’s length transaction at the reporting date.
Diluted earnings per share is computed using the weighted average number of shares and dilutive potential shares except where the result would be anti-dilutive
3.21 Significant Judgements, Assumptions and Estimations in applying Accounting Policies
3.21.1 Leases
The Company evaluates if an arrangement qualifies to be a lease as per the requirements of Ind AS 116. Identification of a lease requires significant judgment. The Company uses significant judgement in assessing the lease term (including anticipated renewals) and the applicable discount rate.
3.21.7 Provisions and Contingencies

3.21.7 Provisions and Contingencies
The assessments undertaken in recognising provisions and contingencies have been made in accordance with Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) 37, ‘Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets’. The evaluation of the likelihood of the contingent events is applied best judgement by management regarding the probability of exposure to potential loss.
3.21.2 Close-down and Restoration Obligations
Close-down and restoration costs are normal consequence of mining or production, and majority of close-down and restoration expenditure are incurred in the years following the closure of mine. Although the ultimate cost to be incurred is uncertain, the Company estimate their costs based on current interpretation of scientific and legal data and existing technology, in addition to assumptions about probability and future costs.

Nature and purpose of other reserves
Capital reserve
Capital reserve is created out of the capital profit, it is created out of the profit earned from some specific transactions of capital nature. Capital reserve is not available for the distribution to the shareholders.
Securities premium
Securities premium represents premium received on issue of shares. The reserve is utilised in accordance with the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.
Bond redemption reserve

Bond redemption reserve
The Group is required to create bond redemption reserve as per the provisions of Companies Act, 2013 out of the profits which are available for distribution of dividends. The reserve is maintained till the redemption of bonds.
Other Comprehensive Income (OCI) reserve
The Group has opted to recognise changes in the fair value of certain investments in equity securities in other comprehensive income. These changes are accumulated within the FVOCI equity investments reserve within equity. The Group transfers amounts from this reserve to retained earnings when the relevant equity securities are derecognised.

(a) Fair value of interest swap is determined based on dealer or counterparty quotes for similar instruments

(c) The carrying value of borrowings bearing variable interest rate are considered to be representative of their fair value.
(d) The carrying value of financial assets and liabilities with maturities less than 12 months are considered to be representative of their fair value.
(e) Fair value of fixed interest rate financial assets and liabilities carried at amortised cost (including lease obligations) is determined by discounting
the cash flows using a discount rate equivalent to market interest rate applicable to similar assets and liabilities as at the balance sheet date.

ii) Risk Management

ii) Risk Management
The Group, its Joint Ventures & Associate is exposed to various risks in relation to financial instruments. The Group, its Joint Ventures & Associate’s financial asset and liabilities by category are summarised in note 43 (i). The main types of risks are market risk, credit risk and liquidity risk. The Group’s, its Joint Venture’s & Associate’s risk management is co-ordinated at its headquarters, in close co-operation with the Board of Directors, and focuses on actively securing the Group’s, its Joint Venture’s & Associate’s short to medium-term cash flows by minimising the exposure to volatile financial markets. Long term financial investments are managed to generate lasting returns. The Group, its Joint Ventures & Associate does not actively engage in the trading of financial assets for speculative purposes nor does it write options. The most significant financial risks to which the Group, its Joint Ventures & Associate is exposed are described below.
A) Credit risk
Consolidated Financial Statements

Consolidated Financial Statements
Credit risk is the risk that a counterparty fails to discharge an obligation to the parent Comapny. The Group, its Joint Ventures & Associate is exposed to this risk for various financial instruments, for example by granting loans and receivables to customers, placing deposits, etc. The Group’s, its Joint Venture’s & Associate’s maximum exposure to credit risk is limited to the carrying amount of following types financial assets.
- Cash and cash equivalents
- Derivative financial instruments
- Trade receivables
- Other financial assets measured at amortized cost
The Group, its Joint Ventures & Associate continuously monitor defaults of customers and other counterparties, identified either individually or by the Group, and incorporates this information into its credit risk controls. Where available at reasonable cost, external credit ratings and/or reports on customers and other counterparties are obtained and used. The Group’s, its Joint Venture’s & Associate’s policy is to deal only with creditworthy counterparties.
a) Credit risk management
Cash and cash equivalent
Credit risk related to cash and cash equivalents is managed by only accepting highly rated banks and diversifying bank deposits and accounts in different banks across the country.
Derivative financial instruments

Derivative financial instruments
Credit risk related to derivative financial instruments is also managed by only entering into such arrangement with highly rated banks or financial institutions as counterparties. The Group, its Joint Ventures & Associate diversifies its holdings with multiple counterparties.
Trade receivables
Credit risk related to trade receivables are mitigated by taking bank guarantees from customers where credit risk is high. The Group, its Joint Ventures & Associate closely monitors the credit-worthiness of the debtors and only sells goods to credit-worthy parties. The Group’s its Joint Venture’s & Associate’s internal systems are configured to define credit limits of customers, thereby limiting the credit risk to pre-calculated amounts.
b) Expected credit losses
Company provides expected credit losses based on the following;
Trade receivables
The Group, its Joint Ventures and Associate recognizes lifetime expected credit losses on trade receivables using a simplified approach and uses historical information to arrive at loss percentage relevant to each category of trade receivables. For descriptive note on trade receivables ageing, refer note 48.4 (B)
Other financial assets measured at amortized cost

Other financial assets measured at amortized cost
Group, its Joint Ventures & Associate provides for expected credit losses on “loans advances and other than trade receivables” by assessing individual financial instruments for expectation of any credit losses. Since this category includes loans and receivables of varied natures and purpose, there is no trend that the Group, its Joint Ventures & Associate can draw to apply consistently to entire population. For such financial assets, the Group’s its Joint Venture’s & Associate’s policy is to provides for 12 month expected credit losses upon initial recognition and provides for lifetime expected credit losses upon significant increase in credit risk. The Group, its Joint Ventures & Associate does not have any expected loss based impairment recognised on such assets considering their low credit risk nature, though incurred loss provisions are disclosed under each sub-category of such financial assets.

B) Liquidity risk

B) Liquidity risk
Prudent liquidity risk management implies maintaining sufficient cash and marketable securities and the availability of funding through an adequate amount of committed credit facilities to meet obligations when due. Due to the nature of the business, the Group, its Joint Ventures & Associate maintain flexibility in funding by maintaining availability under committed facilities. Management monitors rolling forecasts of the Group’s, its Joint Venture’s & Associate’s liquidity position and cash and cash equivalents on the basis of expected cash flows. The Group, its Joint Ventures & Associate takes into account the liquidity of the market in which the entity operates. In addition, the Group’s, its Joint Venture’s & Associate’s liquidity management policy involves projecting cash flows in major currencies and considering the level of liquid assets necessary to meet these, monitoring balance sheet liquidity ratios against internal and external regulatory requirements and maintaining debt financing plans.

C) Market Risk

C) Market Risk
a) Foreign currency risk Most of the Group’s, its Joint Venture’s & Associate’s transactions are carried out in INR. Exposures to currency exchange rates arise from the Group’s, its Joint Venture’s & Associate’s overseas borrowing arrangements, which are primarily denominated in US dollars (USD). To mitigate the Group’s, its Joint Venture’s & Associate’s exposure to foreign currency risk, non-INR cash flows are monitored and forward exchange contracts are entered into in accordance with the Group’s, its Joint Venture’s & Associate’s risk management policies. Generally, the Group’s, its Joint Venture’s & Associate’s risk management procedures distinguish short-term foreign currency cash flows (due within 6 months) from longer-term cash flows (due after 6 months). Where the amounts to be paid and received in a specific currency are expected to largely offset one another, no further hedging activity is undertaken. Forward exchange contracts are mainly entered into for significant long-term foreign currency exposures that are not expected to be offset by other same-currency transactions.

The Bhawanathpur Limestone Mine complex, Garhwa District, Jharkhand, comprises three mining leases — Ghaghra (675.46 ha), Gorgaon (228.46 ha), and Saraiya (275.00 ha). The SAIL Board, in its 442nd meeting held on 30.05.2017, approved the surrender of all three leases to the Government of Jharkhand on account of economic unviability and inability to obtain requisite statutory clearances. The process of formal surrender is under progress with the State Government.

(b) Tulsidamar Dolomite Mine

(b) Tulsidamar Dolomite Mine
The Tulsidamar Dolomite Mine lease (118.72 ha), Garhwa District, Jharkhand, initially granted on 30.10.1969, was last extended up to 31.03.2022 under the Jharkhand Minor Mineral Concession (JMMC) Amendment Rules, 2020. The lease has expired on 31.03.2022, as no statutory provision exists under the JMMC Rules, 2004 for its renewal or further extension. Mining operations at the mine stand suspended since 16.02.2020 following stoppage of transit challan issuance by the District Mining Officer (DMO), Garhwa. In view of the expired lease status, uncompetitive cost economics, and the vacation notice issued by DMO, Garhwa directing handing over of the leasehold area to the State Government, SAIL is under process to formally surrender the Tulsidamar Dolomite Lease.
The requisite Board approval for surrender is presently under consideration.
